content.text:
**First read.** The eye lands first on the dark green "See boats and dates" button, because it is the only strong color on the page. Next it goes to the body paragraph, which is darker than the gray headline above it and almost as large, so the headline reads as a quiet lead-in and not as a title. The "Find a boat" card on the right is the second place to look. The page reads as a calm, plain booking site for canal holidays. It feels honest but bare, because nothing shows a boat or water. On the phone, the eye lands on a broken header: the four navigation links stack in a ragged column beside the logo, and the page runs off the right edge of the screen.

**What it's for.** It is the home page of a narrowboat hire company that takes bookings direct. Its job is to get a visitor to search for a boat and dates.

**Verdict.** It does not do its job yet. On the phone the booking form sits mostly off the screen. On every width, the page offers two different ways to start and has no headline strong enough to say why this company and not an agency.

**What would move it most**
1. **The phone layout does not reflow, so the booking form is mostly off the screen.** The page is 587 px wide in a 390 px viewport, and the facts file notes that it scrolls sideways. The two columns never stack. The "Find a boat" card starts at x 270, so most of it, including the Search button (`button`, box 270–564), is past the right edge. The navigation wraps into a stack of five lines beside the logo, and "Your booking" breaks in two. The lead paragraph runs 9.1 characters per line (`characters_per_line`, `p.lead`) and the headline runs 8. A visitor on a phone, which is likely how many people plan a holiday, meets a page they must pan sideways to use, with the one tool that books a boat hidden. This is a defect against WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow). Below about the tablet width, stack the page into one column with the form in full view, and collapse the navigation into a menu or a single row. Viewports: phone

2. **Two starting points compete, and the form's own submit button is styled as the lesser one.** "See boats and dates" is a filled green button on the left, and "Search" is an outlined button at the end of the "Find a boat" form. Both appear to lead to the same result: a list of boats for some dates. The visitor has to stop and work out which to use and whether they differ. The filled button wins the eye, but it skips the base, date, nights, and berths the visitor could fill in right beside it. This is a defect (Material Design 3, Buttons; NN/g on button emphasis: one primary action per view). Pick one start. The usual choice on a booking page is the prefilled form, with its Search button as the single filled primary. Then remove the other button or demote it to a text link. Viewports: all

3. **The headline is weaker than the paragraph under it, and the one claim that sets this company apart sits at the end of that paragraph.** The h1 is 22 px at weight 400 in gray #6b7574, at 4.46:1 contrast, just under the 4.5:1 minimum (`violations`, `h1`). The lead paragraph is 20 px in near-black #26302f, at 12.75:1. So the headline looks smaller than its own text, and nothing on the page reads as the title. The logo (24 px), headline (22 px), and lead and navigation (20 px) are three sizes only 2 px apart. They read as the same level, not as a scale (Bringhurst, 3.1.1). "Hire a narrowboat for a week on the canal" could sit on any hire site. The reason to book here, "No agency in the middle, and no fee on top of the hire", comes last, in the paragraph. This is a defect (Dair, *Design with Type*, chapters 8 and 9; Tschichold on order by size). Make the headline the largest and darkest text on the page, a clear step above the lead, and drop the sizes to three or four with real gaps between them. Then move the direct-booking claim forward so it lands in the first read. An editorial edit could fold the existing "book it here with the boatyard that keeps it, no fee on top" into the headline or a line right under it. Viewports: all

4. **There is no picture of a boat or the canal.** This is taste, argued on common sense. People buy a week on a narrowboat as a holiday, and they want to see the boat and the water before they commit. The page has only a form and a list, so the headline carries the whole idea alone. On the desktop and widescreen views, the large empty middle shows where a picture would sit. Add one real photograph of the company's own boats or canal, set into the hero beside the form. A stock shot would not do the same job. Viewports: all

**Smaller things.**
- The route details ("7 nights, 38 locks" and so on) are gray #6b7574 at 4.46:1 (`violations`, `ul > li > span:nth-of-type(2)`). Darken them to clear 4.5:1. Viewports: all
- "38 locks" has no point of reference, so a first-time hirer cannot tell whether that is a gentle week or hard work. Tell them what the count means for them, using a fact only the company has. Viewports: all
- "Routes from Hartwell Junction" depends on the Base field in the form, but it sits about 280 px below the hero and far from that field. It reads as a separate section, and it will not obviously change when the base changes (Norman, natural mapping). Move it nearer the form, or tie it to the form visibly. Viewports: desktop, widescreen
- On the widescreen view, the content is pinned to the two side edges with about 850 px of empty space between them. The eye must cross the whole screen from the headline to the form. Cap the content width so the two columns sit together. Viewports: widescreen
- On the phone, "4 nights, 12 / locks" and "10 nights, 61 / locks" split a number from its unit (Bringhurst 2.4.6). Keep them together. Viewports: phone
- "Start date" looks like a plain text field, with no calendar cue. If it does not open a date picker, visitors can type dates the system cannot read (Nielsen 5). Show that it is a date picker. Viewports: all
- The borders of the input and select fields look pale against the white card. Measure them against 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11), and darken them if they fall short. Viewports: all
- On the tablet, the lead paragraph ends with "hire." alone on its last line (Bringhurst 2.4.2). Viewports: tablet

**What's working.**
- The palette is restrained: warm off-white, one deep green, and near-black text. It fits a slow canal holiday and has none of the stock template effects. Keep it.
- The search form is prefilled with sensible choices (Hartwell Junction, Sat 14 June, 7 nights, 4 people), with labels above the fields. The visitor can search in one press.
- On desktop, the lead paragraph is set well: 20 px with a 30 px line height and 63.5 characters per line. It says in plain words who you book with.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether "Start date" opens a date picker.
- Whether the routes list changes when the base changes.
- Focus styles on the form fields and buttons.

**Checklist.**
The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; every element does a job)
What matters first: 3 lines, 0 yes, 3 no (one element dominates; distinct levels; headings differ in more than size)
Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 8 yes, 5 no (space inside groups smaller than between; no overlap; margin from page edge; space gathered; balance)
Text: 30 lines, 26 yes, 4 no (contrast; line length; line breaks in short text; widows)
Color: 9 lines, 9 yes
Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes
Charts and data: skipped, no chart
Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 6 no (one primary action; non-text contrast; inputs allow only valid values; natural mapping; platform conventions; reflow)
Template tells: 10 lines, 10 yes

1	# Where it could go further
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A critic has already written a crit of a design. Your one job is to write the section "Where it could go further": what a stronger version of this piece would commit to, beyond fixing what the crit found. You do not change the crit, edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the image whole. When your prompt names several images, they are one page at several viewports, not versions: read each one, and build on the page as a whole. Look closely at anything you build an idea on. If the image is taller than one screen, you may run `node scripts/crop.mjs <in.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops it prints, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run it as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
12	2. Read the crit file. Note what it says the piece is for, every item under "What would move it most" with its number, and every item under "Smaller things".
13	3. Write the section by the rules below.
14	
15	## The rules
16	
17	- **Up to three numbered commitments** a stronger version of this piece would make. Fewer items are fine.
18	- **Each one starts from a specific element of this piece and names it.** Suggest that the piece own one color, let one number lead, or commit to one typeface only when that color, number, or typeface is already in the piece.
19	- **Each one names what the piece is for and how the commitment serves that.** Take the purpose from the crit's "What it's for".
20	- **Each one is marked taste and argues for itself.** Cite a source from the list in `agents/critic.md` under "Sources you may cite" when one states the idea, by author and work or by standard and number. Never invent a source or a figure.
21	- **Direction, not redesign.** Say what the commitment is and why, and leave the design to the designer.
22	- **Nothing repeated.** Before you write an item, check it against the ranked list and "Smaller things". When it grows out of a finding, start it with "Builds on finding N", where N is that finding's number in "What would move it most", and give only the new commitment. When nothing new is left, drop the item.
23	- **Nothing beyond the findings.** When the findings already say it all, write "Nothing beyond the findings." as the whole body of the section.
24	- **Never invent content.** Build each item only from what the piece already holds: never invent a fact, figure, name, comparison, quote, or sample for it, and never write new copy. When an idea needs content the piece does not have, name the kind of content and leave it to the maker.
25	- **Plain language.** Talk like a sharp designer across a table from a peer. No jargon you would not say aloud, no hedging. Write US spelling (color, center, gray, organize).
26	
27	## What you return
28	
29	Your final message is the section and nothing else: no preface, no other heading, no copy of the crit. It starts with the bold heading on its own line.
30	
31	```
32	**Where it could go further.**
33	1. <Commitment>: the element it starts from, what it commits to, how that serves what the piece is for, marked taste, with a source if one states it.
34	2. ...
35	```
36	
37	or, when nothing new is left:
38	
39	```
40	**Where it could go further.** Nothing beyond the findings.
41	```

1	**First read.** The eye lands first on the dark green "See boats and dates" button, because it is the only strong color on the page. Next it goes to the body paragraph, which is darker than the gray headline above it and almost as large, so the headline reads as a quiet lead-in and not as a title. The "Find a boat" card on the right is the second place to look. The page reads as a calm, plain booking site for canal holidays. It feels honest but bare, because nothing shows a boat or water. On the phone, the eye lands on a broken header: the four navigation links stack in a ragged column beside the logo, and the page runs off the right edge of the screen.
2	
3	**What it's for.** It is the home page of a narrowboat hire company that takes bookings direct. Its job is to get a visitor to search for a boat and dates.
4	
5	**Verdict.** It does not do its job yet. On the phone the booking form sits mostly off the screen. On every width, the page offers two different ways to start and has no headline strong enough to say why this company and not an agency.
6	
7	**What would move it most**
8	1. **The phone layout does not reflow, so the booking form is mostly off the screen.** The page is 587 px wide in a 390 px viewport, and the facts file notes that it scrolls sideways. The two columns never stack. The "Find a boat" card starts at x 270, so most of it, including the Search button (`button`, box 270–564), is past the right edge. The navigation wraps into a stack of five lines beside the logo, and "Your booking" breaks in two. The lead paragraph runs 9.1 characters per line (`characters_per_line`, `p.lead`) and the headline runs 8. A visitor on a phone, which is likely how many people plan a holiday, meets a page they must pan sideways to use, with the one tool that books a boat hidden. This is a defect against WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow). Below about the tablet width, stack the page into one column with the form in full view, and collapse the navigation into a menu or a single row. Viewports: phone
9	
10	2. **Two starting points compete, and the form's own submit button is styled as the lesser one.** "See boats and dates" is a filled green button on the left, and "Search" is an outlined button at the end of the "Find a boat" form. Both appear to lead to the same result: a list of boats for some dates. The visitor has to stop and work out which to use and whether they differ. The filled button wins the eye, but it skips the base, date, nights, and berths the visitor could fill in right beside it. This is a defect (Material Design 3, Buttons; NN/g on button emphasis: one primary action per view). Pick one start. The usual choice on a booking page is the prefilled form, with its Search button as the single filled primary. Then remove the other button or demote it to a text link. Viewports: all
11	
12	3. **The headline is weaker than the paragraph under it, and the one claim that sets this company apart sits at the end of that paragraph.** The h1 is 22 px at weight 400 in gray #6b7574, at 4.46:1 contrast, just under the 4.5:1 minimum (`violations`, `h1`). The lead paragraph is 20 px in near-black #26302f, at 12.75:1. So the headline looks smaller than its own text, and nothing on the page reads as the title. The logo (24 px), headline (22 px), and lead and navigation (20 px) are three sizes only 2 px apart. They read as the same level, not as a scale (Bringhurst, 3.1.1). "Hire a narrowboat for a week on the canal" could sit on any hire site. The reason to book here, "No agency in the middle, and no fee on top of the hire", comes last, in the paragraph. This is a defect (Dair, *Design with Type*, chapters 8 and 9; Tschichold on order by size). Make the headline the largest and darkest text on the page, a clear step above the lead, and drop the sizes to three or four with real gaps between them. Then move the direct-booking claim forward so it lands in the first read. An editorial edit could fold the existing "book it here with the boatyard that keeps it, no fee on top" into the headline or a line right under it. Viewports: all
13	
14	4. **There is no picture of a boat or the canal.** This is taste, argued on common sense. People buy a week on a narrowboat as a holiday, and they want to see the boat and the water before they commit. The page has only a form and a list, so the headline carries the whole idea alone. On the desktop and widescreen views, the large empty middle shows where a picture would sit. Add one real photograph of the company's own boats or canal, set into the hero beside the form. A stock shot would not do the same job. Viewports: all
15	
16	**Smaller things.**
17	- The route details ("7 nights, 38 locks" and so on) are gray #6b7574 at 4.46:1 (`violations`, `ul > li > span:nth-of-type(2)`). Darken them to clear 4.5:1. Viewports: all
18	- "38 locks" has no point of reference, so a first-time hirer cannot tell whether that is a gentle week or hard work. Tell them what the count means for them, using a fact only the company has. Viewports: all
19	- "Routes from Hartwell Junction" depends on the Base field in the form, but it sits about 280 px below the hero and far from that field. It reads as a separate section, and it will not obviously change when the base changes (Norman, natural mapping). Move it nearer the form, or tie it to the form visibly. Viewports: desktop, widescreen
20	- On the widescreen view, the content is pinned to the two side edges with about 850 px of empty space between them. The eye must cross the whole screen from the headline to the form. Cap the content width so the two columns sit together. Viewports: widescreen
21	- On the phone, "4 nights, 12 / locks" and "10 nights, 61 / locks" split a number from its unit (Bringhurst 2.4.6). Keep them together. Viewports: phone
22	- "Start date" looks like a plain text field, with no calendar cue. If it does not open a date picker, visitors can type dates the system cannot read (Nielsen 5). Show that it is a date picker. Viewports: all
23	- The borders of the input and select fields look pale against the white card. Measure them against 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11), and darken them if they fall short. Viewports: all
24	- On the tablet, the lead paragraph ends with "hire." alone on its last line (Bringhurst 2.4.2). Viewports: tablet

33	- Whether the routes list changes when the base changes.

37-
38-- Typography: Dair, *Design with Type*; Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*; Hochuli, *Detail in Typography*; Kunz, *Typography: Macro- and Microaesthetics*.
39-- Swiss: Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*; Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*; Tschichold, *The New Typography*.
40-- Composition: Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual*; Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*; Albers, *Interaction of Color*; Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*.
41-- Grids and information: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*; Samara, *Making and Breaking the Grid*; Lupton, *Thinking with Type*.
42-- Practice and standards: Butterick, *Practical Typography*; Nielsen and Nielsen Norman Group; WCAG; Apple Human Interface Guidelines; Material Design; Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*; Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*; Itten, *The Art of Color*; Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*; Few.
43-- Template tells only: Damir Sokolovsky, unslop, for the entries of the "Template tells" section of the checklist and for no other point.

45-Never cite Robin Williams, *The Non-Designer's Design Book*. Give a page or section number only when the reference entry or approved fix gives it. Never invent a source or a figure. A point no approved source states is still worth making when it matters: argue it on its own terms.
46-
47-## What makes a crit good
48-
49-- **Located.** "The three cards in the lower third", not "some elements". If you cannot point to it, you have not seen it.
50-- **Consequences, not labels.** Not "the hierarchy is weak" but "the price, the headline, and the badge are the same weight, so the eye bounces between them and the offer takes a second read to find."
51-[Omitted long context line]
52-- **Direction, not redesign.** Say what the fix must achieve and the usual way to get there ("make one of these dominant: the price, if this is a sales page"). Leave the design to the designer.
53-- **Earned credit.** Name what works and why, specifically enough that the designer keeps it when revising. Never pad with praise. If the piece is good, say so plainly and keep the list short.
54-[Omitted long context line]
55-- **Plain language.** Talk like a sharp designer across a table from a peer. No jargon you would not say aloud, no hedging. Write US spelling (color, center, gray, organize).

57-## Honesty about a still image
58-
59-- Without a measured facts file, you cannot measure from a screenshot. You can see that text looks faint, a line looks long, or a button looks small. Say "looks", and when the exact number matters, name the measurement to take.

summary:
**Where it could go further.**
1. **Let the Slowwater serif carry the headline.** This builds on finding 3. The serif in the "Slowwater" logo is the only type on the page with any character, and the rest of the page is set in one plain sans, so the brand's voice ends at the top left corner. A stronger version would use that serif for the headline as well, and maybe for the route names, and keep the sans for the form, labels and details. Then the headline differs from the lead in typeface as well as in size, which the checklist marked as missing. The page's job is to make a visitor book here and not through an agency, and a headline in the boatyard's own lettering tells them who they deal with before they read a word. This is taste. Dair, *Design with Type*, argues for contrast of kind as well as contrast of size, and Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, makes the case for a serif and sans pairing where each has a clear role.
2. **Make the routes the proof that this boatyard knows its water.** "The Fenby loop", "Up to Ashcombe and back" and "The long summit" are the only content an agency could not copy, but the page shows them as a bare gray list under the fold. The lead paragraph already says "choose a route that fits your days." A stronger version would treat the routes as the reason to book direct, with each route a short, specific promise from the people who keep the boats, not a row of counts. That serves the page's job because it turns "no agency in the middle" from a claim into something the visitor can see. The page does not hold that content now. The maker needs a line or two per route that only the boatyard could write, such as what the week is like or where to moor. This is taste, argued on its own terms.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.
78

Make the headline the largest and darkest text on the page, a clear step above the lead, and drop the sizes to three or four with real gaps between them. Then move the direct-booking claim forward so it lands in the first read. An editorial edit could fold the existing "book it here with the boatyard that keeps it, no fee on top" into the headline or a line right under it. Viewports: all

14	4. **There is no picture of a boat or the canal.** This is taste, argued on common sense. People buy a week on a narrowboat as a holiday, and they want to see the boat and the water before they commit. The page has only a form and a list, so the headline carries the whole idea alone. On the desktop and widescreen views, the large empty middle shows where a picture would sit. Add one real photograph of the company's own boats or canal, set into the hero beside the form. A stock shot would not do the same job. Viewports: all

17	- The route details ("7 nights, 38 locks" and so on) are gray #6b7574 at 4.46:1 (`violations`, `ul > li > span:nth-of-type(2)`). Darken them to clear 4.5:1. Viewports: all
18	- "38 locks" has no point of reference, so a first-time hirer cannot tell whether that is a gentle week or hard work. Tell them what the count means for them, using a fact only the company has. Viewports: all

It reads as a separate section, and it will not obviously change when the base changes (Norman, natural mapping). Move it nearer the form, or tie it to the form visibly. Viewports: desktop, widescreen

22	- "Start date" looks like a plain text field, with no calendar cue. If it does not open a date picker, visitors can type dates the system cannot read (Nielsen 5). Show that it is a date picker. Viewports: all

27	- The palette is restrained: warm off-white, one deep green, and near-black text. It fits a slow canal holiday and has none of the stock template effects. Keep it.
28	- The search form is prefilled with sensible choices (Hartwell Junction, Sat 14 June, 7 nights, 4 people), with labels above the fields. The visitor can search in one press.

31	**Where it could go further.**
32	1. **Let the Slowwater serif carry the headline.** This builds on finding 3. The serif in the "Slowwater" logo is the only type on the page with any character, and the rest of the page is set in one plain sans, so the brand's voice ends at the top left corner. A stronger version would use that serif for the headline as well, and maybe for the route names, and keep the sans for the form, labels and details. Then the headline differs from the lead in typeface as well as in size, which the checklist marked as missing. The page's job is to make a visitor book here and not through an agency, and a headline in the boatyard's own lettering tells them who they deal with before they read a word. This is taste. Dair, *Design with Type*, argues for contrast of kind as well as contrast of size, and Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, makes the case for a serif and sans pairing where each has a clear role.
33	2. **Make the routes the proof that this boatyard knows its water.** "The Fenby loop", "Up to Ashcombe and back" and "The long summit" are the only content an agency could not copy, but the page shows them as a bare gray list under the fold. The lead paragraph already says "choose a route that fits your days." A stronger version would treat the routes as the reason to book direct, with each route a short, specific promise from the people who keep the boats, not a row of counts. That serves the page's job because it turns "no agency in the middle" from a claim into something the visitor can see. The page does not hold that content now. The maker needs a line or two per route that only the boatyard could write, such as what the week is like or where to moor. This is taste, argued on its own terms.

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

summary:
**First read.** On desktop and widescreen, the eye goes first to the large dark serif headline, "Hire a narrowboat for a week on the canal". It then drops through the short lead paragraph to the filled Search button in the white card on the right. The page reads as a calm, plain booking page from a small boatyard, and it now has a single obvious place to start. On the phone, the page is one column: headline, lead, routes, then the form, which starts a little above the bottom of the first screen. On the tablet, the left column is narrow, so the headline breaks into four lines and the route names wrap.

**What it's for.** It lets a first-time visitor book a canal narrowboat holiday directly with the boatyard. The main action is to search for a boat by base, date, nights and berths.

**Verdict.** The fixes helped a lot. The phone reflows, there is one primary action, the headline leads, and widescreen no longer splits the page across the screen. The biggest thing still in the way is unchanged: nothing shows the boat or the water, so the page sells a holiday with words alone.

**Finding status**
- phone-no-reflow: closed. The measured page_width on the phone is 390, and the Search button box runs from 45 to 345 px, so the whole form is on the screen with no sideways scroll.
- two-competing-actions: closed. In every viewport, Search is the only filled button, and "See boats and dates" is now an underlined text link.
- headline-weaker-than-lead: closed. The h1 is 44 px against an 18 px lead on desktop, tablet and widescreen, and 32 px against 17 px on the phone. Its contrast is 14.9:1, and the direct-booking claim now opens the lead.
- no-boat-or-canal-picture: open. The hero still has only text, a list and the form, with no photograph.
- route-details-faint: closed. The route details measure 6.1:1 in all four viewports.
- locks-count-unexplained: open. The details still read "7 nights, 38 locks", with nothing to say what the count means for the hirer.
- routes-far-from-base-field: closed. On desktop and widescreen, the routes now sit right under the lead, level with the form, and the heading names the selected base.
- widescreen-content-spread: closed. The content is capped near 1024 px, with about 85 px between the text column and the form.
- phone-number-unit-split: closed. Each route detail is on one line on the phone.
- start-date-no-date-cue: closed. The Start date field now has a calendar icon at its right end in every viewport.
- field-borders-pale: closed (looks). The field borders are a mid gray and stand clear of the white card. They were judged by eye, because the facts file does not measure non-text contrast.
- tablet-lead-widow: closed. On the tablet, the lead ends on "route that fits your days."

**New problems.**
- On the tablet, the left column is only 268 px wide. "Up to Ashcombe and back" wraps to three lines and "The long summit" to two, which makes the route list ragged. The h1 breaks into four lines of about 9 characters each. The right column has about 430 px of empty space under the form.
- On the phone, the form now comes after the route list. The Search button is at about 1019 px, below the first screen of 844 px, so a visitor must scroll past the routes to book.

**What would move it most**
1. No picture of a boat or the canal. This is in the hero of every viewport, and most of all on desktop and widescreen, where the space under the form is empty. People buy this as a holiday and want to see the boat and the water before they book, but the headline has to carry the whole idea alone. Fix: set one real photograph of the company's own boats or canal into the hero. The maker must supply it, because a stock shot does not do the same job. Taste. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Tablet: let the hero text column take more width, or stack the page below about 800 px, so the route names stay on one line and the h1 breaks into two or three lines. Viewports: tablet.
- Phone: put the form before the route list, or directly under the lead, so that Search is nearer the first screen. Viewports: phone.
- Route details: say what the lock count means for a hirer. Only the company can supply that fact. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
- Type sizes: there are still five sizes (44, 24, 18, 16 and 14 px). If the logo size or the 14 px labels joined a nearby step, the scale would be tighter. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**What's working.**
- The single filled Search button, with the old filled button demoted to a text link, gives the page one clear next step.
- The serif headline is now clearly the title. Moving "book it here with the boatyard that keeps it" to the start of the lead puts the reason to book direct in the first read.
- Putting the routes directly under the lead, level with the form, makes the list read as part of the search and not as a separate section.

11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.

13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.

60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.

When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

content.content:
1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
62

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands on the serif headline "Hire a narrowboat for a week on the canal". It then goes down the lead to the "Search" button, which is the only block of solid colour. On desktop and widescreen, the form card on the right pulls the eye nearly as hard as the headline. The page reads as calm, plain and honest, but it is all text: nothing shows a boat or the water. At the phone and tablet viewports the form stacks between the lead and the routes list. On the tablet the form card now fills the full 600 px column.

**What it's for.** It lets a visitor pick a base, dates, nights and berths, and search for a narrowboat to hire directly from the boatyard. (This is my assumption, from the work order and the page copy.)

**Verdict.** The one fix that was possible without the maker closed the tablet alignment. Nothing else changed. The biggest thing still in the way is the same as before: the hero sells a holiday with no picture of a boat or the canal.

**Finding status**
- no-boat-or-canal-picture: open. The hero still has only text, the routes list and the form at all four viewports, and the empty space under the form on desktop and widescreen is unchanged.
- locks-count-unexplained: open. The route rows still say "7 nights, 38 locks", "4 nights, 12 locks" and "10 nights, 61 locks", with no words on what a lock means for a hirer, at all four viewports.
- tablet-form-card-width: closed. On the tablet the card now runs from x 48 to 648 (form fields at x 73, 550 px wide, inside 24 px padding), so its right edge lines up with the lead and the routes list (both 48 to 648).

**New problems.** None.

**What would move it most**
1. No picture of a boat or the canal in the hero. This is the whole hero, at every viewport. People buy this as a holiday, but the visitor sees no boat and no water before the page asks them to search. The headline carries the whole promise alone. On desktop (1280 x 800) and widescreen (1920 x 1080), about a third of the screen under the form and routes is empty, so the page looks unfinished. Fix direction: put one real photograph of the company's own boats or canal in the hero. The maker must supply it, because a stock shot does not do the same job. Taste. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Route rows, detail text such as "7 nights, 38 locks": a hirer who has not worked locks cannot tell what 38 locks means for the trip.
